# Discover (prior art): a cosy game about running a lighthouse

Made by the BMUZ research flow: four lenses (Mainstream, Extremes & failures, Outside the field, Disconfirm), each working alone, merged after. Strength: (several sources) = two or more different sites agree · (one source) · (interpretation only) = a helper's reading. Nothing here is a decision: choosing is /define's. The bricks below join the project's .planning/DISCOVER.md.

Where each lens stopped (saturation or the cap):
Mainstream: Stopped at nothing new. 4 pages fetched and 4 searches run: Steam Lighthouse Keeper, Steam Keeper, Shacknews Static Dread review, adventuregamehotspot The Lightkeeper review. The last searches repeated known titles and added no new mechanics. Several claims come only from search snippets (flagged 'unverified' above). Cap of 6 sources not reached.
Extremes & failures: Six pages were opened (Keeper review on player2, Cagibi postmortem, Keeper Lit page, The Wickie page, The Twin Geeks review, TechRadar Keeper review). The TechRadar page returned only its headline, so it is not cited. Five sources were used. Stopped at the six-source cap; the last searches added little new, and no source on chore or boredom complaints in the lighthouse genre was found beyond these.
Outside the field: Six sources, the cap, so I stopped at the cap rather than at nothing new. The last two fetches (Britannica, returned 403, and the NPS volunteer page) added little; the Ponce Inlet PDF came from a search snippet only and was not opened. Gaps: Keeper's review body (TechRadar returned only the headline) and any Steam review text for Lighthouse Keeper, so praise and complaints remain thin. Fear 1 and fear 3 have only indirect evidence.
Disconfirm: Opened 5 sources (cap is 6). Stopped because the remaining search hits were aggregator pages with scores and no review text, so further fetches would add labels and not complaint text. Stopped at nothing new on complaints; the last source added only the crafting description and the Very Positive label.

## Question
- Research: Prior art — games that already do this, or part of it: what each shares with the bricks collected, what players praise, what they complain about or say is missing, and the hook (the part players have never seen) and anchor (the familiar part) each uses. Also twists: what taking something away, an odd mashup or an extreme would do
- The idea, in the creative's words: a cosy game about running a lighthouse
- Who the player is: You are a lighthouse keeper looking after a light on a quiet coast.
- Must fit / off the table: Cosy tone: no timers that punish, no failure states.; Browser-first, to fit the usual BMUZ web stack (React, Three.js). Platform still open to /define.
- Fears and assumptions: "It becomes a chore with nothing to look forward to." (important, desirable, a fear); "Too little to do, so the cosy feel turns into boredom." (important, viable, a fear); "Hard to keep the light and the sea reading clearly on a phone screen." (important, feasible, a fear)

## Research questions
1. Which games are closest to this idea, and which of its bricks do they share?
2. What do players praise in them, and what do they complain about or say is missing?
3. What hooks and anchors do those games use, and what twists has nobody tried?

## Findings by question
### 1. Which games are closest to this idea, and which of its bricks do they share?
**The closest sourced games each share a different subset of the lighthouse bricks**
- Keeper (Double Fine, 2025) is the closest shipped game to the lamp-as-character and light-aiming bricks: the lighthouse is an animated character and the beam is aimed in play. [1][2][3] (several sources)
- Static Dread: The Lighthouse shares the lamp and lens going out, the rotating light, generator upkeep, daytime repairs, the night shift, ship guidance by radio and rule sheets. [4][5] (several sources)
- Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera, 2022) shares the resource haul, crafting, cooking, sailing and farming bricks; whether it also shares the lighthouse upkeep brick is read two different ways (see contradictions). [6][7] (one source)
- Keeper Lit (Lapwing Studio, in development) shares lamp and lens maintenance, generator and fuel checks, fog warning systems and storm preparation, with supplies arriving only by automated drone. [8] (one source)
- The Wickie shares fuelling the generator to keep the light working, guiding lost ships with the light, radio distress calls and sleeping as a day advance. [9] (one source)
- Little Lighthouse of Horror shares kerosene refills at the lamp, a beam that signals ships, and weekly supply orders. [10] (one source)
- Lighthouse Keeper (Cagibi, a shooter) uses the lighthouse as a beam the player fires. [11] (one source)
- The Lightkeeper shares routine lighthouse duties and light exploration. [12] (one source)
- Taken together, no single sourced game covers the lamp, the lens, the clockwork weight and the fog bell in one loop; each source covers a different part. [1][8][6][4] (interpretation only)
**Two bricks have little or no game precedent in these sources**
- A hand-wound clockwork weight that drives the lens does not appear in any sourced game; it appears only in the record of the real keepers' job. [13][8] (interpretation only)
- A fog bell or fog signal appears in a sourced game only as Keeper Lit's fog warning systems, with no timed bell pattern described. [8] (one source)
### 2. What do players praise in them, and what do they complain about or say is missing?
**Players praise mood, freedom from failure, and clear endings**
- Keeper is praised for letting players explore at their own pace with no fail state, and for the animation of the lighthouse and bird. [2] (one source)
- Keeper's store page shows 91% of 1,088 reviews positive and critic blurbs of 'fresh and inventive' and 'a psychedelic exploration of life'. [1] (one source)
- Keeper is praised for a 'no hand holding' style and for fun puzzles, and a TechRadar headline calls it 'bold, bright' (headline only, body not read). [3][14] (several sources)
- Static Dread is praised for holding attention and for never overstaying its welcome. [4] (one source)
- Static Dread's reviewer says it ends at the right time, before it becomes too repetitive. [5] (one source)
- The Lightkeeper is praised for atmosphere, immersive graphics and endings described as logical conclusions. [12] (one source)
- The Wickie is praised for elegant simplicity, monochrome pixel art, and resource management that grows into engagement once understood. [9] (one source)
- Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera) has a 'Very Positive' label from 338 Steam reviews (80% positive), and steambase shows 'Mostly Positive' from 427 reviews. [7][15] (several sources)
**Players complain about chores with no visible purpose, thin challenge, and hard-to-read controls**
- The Lightkeeper's listed drawbacks are mostly mundane chores and light exploration, a slow first half, and simple, mostly inventory-based puzzles. [12] (one source)
- Search snippets (not opened) for Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera) say there is no real incentive to tend the lighthouse beyond self-imposed goals, that crafting is thin, and that duties feel pointless. [16][7][15] (several sources)
- Search snippets (not opened) for Static Dread say it settles into monotony, and that its upkeep chores feel repetitive and like chores. [16] (one source)
- Static Dread's reviewer found tracking the nightly rules 'needlessly frustrating', had no peripheral vision while drawing courses, and called the job lonely. [5] (one source)
- Keeper's reviewer says it 'gives very little instruction on what your next move should be', asked for clearer indication of when to act, and found the beam 'a little finicky moment to moment' and early movement 'a little clunky'. [2] (one source)
- Keeper's reviewer called it 'not exactly a complex game' with 'too simple' first impressions, found the opening 'was just walking', called the fixed camera 'a slight hindrance', and felt 'a tiny smidge of dissatisfaction' at the ending. [3] (one source)
- A TechRadar headline says Keeper is 'lacking a little in depth' (headline only, body not read). [14] (one source)
- The Wickie does not feel very interactive at first, and most runs end with the player missing one meter. [9] (one source)
- Cagibi's postmortem says the beginning can be easy and boring, players spammed the lighthouse special attack, and a healing shot was cut because players spammed it. [11] (one source)
**Player counts do not show that players are bored**
- Gamereactor reports Keeper had 'only 140 active players' at time of writing and a peak of 165 at launch, but gives no cause and suggests marketing or concept fit as possibilities. [17] (one source)
- Low player counts are not evidence that the game is boring, because the article itself names marketing or concept fit as possible causes. [17] (interpretation only)
### 3. What hooks and anchors do those games use, and what twists has nobody tried?
**Familiar anchors players already recognise**
- Static Dread's familiar part is a day and night routine: repair, greet and clean by day, then stay awake through the night shift. [4] (interpretation only)
- Keeper Lit's familiar part is a daily checklist of duties: lamp, generator, fuel and water. [8] (interpretation only)
- Keeper's familiar part is a walk-look-and-solve puzzle adventure with a companion bird. [1][3] (interpretation only)
- Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera)'s familiar part is island survival: farming, fishing and relaxed tags. [6] (interpretation only)
- The real keepers' job had a 4-hour night watch for each keeper, rotated daily between them. [13] (one source)
**Hooks that players have not seen in this form yet**
- Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera)'s hook is the trip out: sailing to other islands for supplies, not only the tower. [6] (interpretation only)
- Keeper's hook is the lamp as a tool that burns away corruption, with a bird helping with objects. [3][1] (interpretation only)
- The Wickie's hook is finding a passing ship's place on its route by counting dots, not from a map. [9] (interpretation only)
- Keeper Lit's hook is that supplies arrive only by automated drone, so the keeper never leaves the tower. [8] (interpretation only)
- Static Dread's hook is the lighthouse as a radio post where the keeper guides ships by radio at night, in an eldritch horror setting. [5] (interpretation only)
- Cagibi's hook is the lighthouse fired as a beam attack, which must carry a cost to stop spam. [11] (interpretation only)
**A real light's identity is its flash rhythm, drawn from a small shared set**
- Each real lighthouse is identified by a pattern of flashes per period, or by colour; for example Pigeon Point flashes once every ten seconds. [18] (one source)
- Light patterns are governed by international agreement and the number of characters is restricted; in 1880s California seventeen different characteristics were used. [18] (one source)
- Notation such as 'Gp Oc(3) W 10s' gives a light's group, colour and period. [18] (one source)
- Two neighbouring lights must not share a rhythm, so the number of distinct rhythms limits how many lights can share a coast. [18] (interpretation only)
### Beyond the questions
**The real keepers' jobs and tending rituals are a ready-made source of anchors**
- Keepers hand-carried fuel to the lantern room, trimmed wicks, and polished the glass chimney, lenses and windows with jeweler's rouge and whiting. [13] (one source)
- Keepers cleaned and lubricated the clockwork, cranked up the weight, latched it, and released it when they lit the lamp at night. [13] (one source)
- Keepers wrote reports, kept records and ordered supplies. [13] (one source)
- The Cape Hatteras volunteer page offers only 'assisting with lighthouse climbs' for lighthouses, with no light-maintenance or keeper-style tasks for the public. [19] (one source)
**Routine toys and lighthouse-as-tool lessons show that attachment can spill over and that signals get spammed**
- Tamagotchi owners cared for the pet in real time; the pet followed a daily rhythm and slept at night, and neglect led to death; children felt attached and a sense of loss. [20] (one source)
- Children brought the toys to school so often that the school banned them, and children asked their parents to care for the pets during the day. [20] (one source)
- Cagibi's postmortem says players spammed the lighthouse special attack, so the lighthouse was made to take damage to stop attack spam and camping behind it. [11] (one source)
- In Static Dread the lights randomly go out and the generator periodically shuts off, with rising intensity, so power failure is the recurring threat. [4] (one source)

## Bricks
### Prior art
- Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera, 2022) · shares: lighthouse as base, repairing its mechanisms, crafting, cooking, resource haul, sailing, farm · praised for: 80% of 338 Steam reviews positive, 'Very Positive' label; steambase shows 'Mostly Positive' from 427 · complaints / missed: 'no real incentive' to tend the lighthouse and thin crafting (search snippets, not opened) · hook / anchor: hook = sailing to 11 islands; anchor = farm and fish [6][7][16][15] (several sources)
- Keeper (Double Fine, 2025) · shares: lamp as a character, light aimed in play, companion bird, wordless story · praised for: 91% of 1,088 store reviews positive; 'fresh and inventive' and 'a psychedelic exploration of life' (store blurbs); freedom with no fail state; animation of lighthouse and bird; 'no hand holding'; 'bold, bright' (TechRadar headline) · complaints / missed: clunky early movement, finicky beam, little guidance on the next move, unclear when to act, too simple, passive walking opening, fixed camera, ending dissatisfaction, 'lacking a little in depth' (TechRadar headline) · hook / anchor: hook = the lamp as companion and tool; anchor = walk-and-solve adventure [1][2][3][17][14] (several sources)
- Static Dread: The Lighthouse · shares: lamp and lens going out, rotating light, generator upkeep, daytime repairs, keeper on the night shift, ship guidance, rule sheets · praised for: 'never overstayed its welcome'; ends at the right time; tense decisions; atmosphere · complaints / missed: rules hard to track and 'needlessly frustrating'; lonely, repetitive rooms; daytime chores that feel like chores (snippet, unverified); no peripheral vision while drawing routes; 'settling into monotony' (snippet) · hook / anchor: hook = horror overlay and the lighthouse as an eldritch radio post; anchor = day/night routine and Papers Please-style rule sheets [4][5][16] (several sources)
- The Lightkeeper · shares: routine lighthouse duties, light exploration · praised for: atmosphere, immersive graphics, endings described as logical conclusions (80% review) · complaints / missed: 'mostly mundane chores and light exploration', slow first half, simple inventory-based puzzles · hook / anchor: hook = atmosphere; anchor = mundane chores [12] (one source)
- Keeper Lit (Lapwing Studio, in development) · shares: lamp and lens maintenance, generator and fuel checks, water and heating upkeep, undersea cable monitoring, fog warning systems, storm and outage prep · praised for: none shown on the page · complaints / missed: no player reaction on record; reads as a daily checklist · hook / anchor: anchor = daily duty list; hook = supplies arrive only by automated drone [8] (one source)
- The Wickie (Dashing Ashes, Ludum Dare 49) · shares: fuel the generator to keep the light working, guiding lost ships with the light, radio distress calls, sleep as a day advance · praised for: elegant simplicity, monochrome pixel art, resource management that grows into engagement · complaints / missed: not interactive at first; most runs end missing one meter; clunky English lines · hook / anchor: hook = finding a ship's place on its route by counting dots; anchor = radio distress call [9] (one source)
- Little Lighthouse of Horror (The Twin Geeks review) · shares: kerosene refill at the lamp, beam signalling ships, weekly supply orders, keeping the beam moving · praised for: not captured on the page · complaints / missed: death or dismissal on failure, which breaks the no-punishment rule · hook / anchor: hook = a survival stat (sanity) tied to a lamp; anchor = weekly supply order [10] (one source)
- Lighthouse Keeper (Cagibi, shooter) · shares: lighthouse as a tool the player fires · praised for: the lighthouse special attack is fun · complaints / missed: players spam it; the lighthouse gets in the way; easy, boring opening; a healing shot had to be cut · hook / anchor: anchor = lighthouse as a beam weapon; hook = a cost on the signal, not on the keeper [11] (one source)
- Tamagotchi (Yokoi, 1996, non-game toy) · shares: a needy thing on a day-and-night clock, tended in real time · praised for: children felt attached and a sense of loss · complaints / missed: over-investment; teachers annoyed; school ban; children asked parents to care for pets during the day · hook / anchor: hook = the pet sleeps at night so the owner's chores follow its clock; anchor = a pet's needs [20] (one source)
### Hooks & anchors
- Anchor: a day-and-night routine of repair, greet and clean by day, then stay awake through the night shift (Static Dread). [4] (one source)
- Anchor: a daily checklist of lamp, generator, fuel and water duties (Keeper Lit). [8] (one source)
- Hook: supplies arrive only by automated drone, so the keeper never leaves the tower (Keeper Lit). [8] (one source)
- Hook: a trip out to other islands for supplies, not only the tower (Lighthouse Keeper, Stratera). [6] (one source)
- Anchor: island survival with farming and fishing (Lighthouse Keeper, Stratera). [6] (one source)
- Hook: the lamp as a tool that burns away corruption, with a bird companion helping with objects (Keeper). [3][1] (several sources)
- Anchor: a walk-look-and-solve adventure with a companion that Keeper players already know. [3] (one source)
- Hook: finding a ship's place on its route by counting dots, not from a map (The Wickie). [9] (one source)
- Hook: nightly radio guidance of ships from the lighthouse, in place of walking on foot (Static Dread). [5] (one source)
- Hook: a clear end length, so the tending game stops before repetition sets in (Static Dread's reviewer praised this). [5] (one source)
- Anchor: the real keeper's 4-hour night watch, rotated daily between keepers. [13] (one source)
- Anchor: the real keeper's jobs of fuelling the lamp, trimming wicks, polishing the glass, cleaning the clockwork and writing reports. [13] (one source)
- Hook: the clockwork ritual, where the weight is wound and released at the moment the lamp is lit, so the start of the light is itself a small action. [13] (one source)
- Hook: a light's identity is its flash rhythm, from a small shared set of patterns fixed by international agreement. [18] (one source)
### Twists
- Twist, take away: remove the day chores and make the night at the lamp the whole game, one short night per play. [5] (one source)
- Twist, take away: the player never sees the lamp or the sea and learns only from the logbook and ships' reactions. [13] (one source)
- Twist, take away: the ship never says whether it read the signal; the only feedback is its heading changing. [17] (one source)
- Mashup: Keeper's walking lighthouse plus Static Dread's day/night routine, with the lighthouse taking the trip to meet ships. [1][4] (several sources)
- Mashup: the Tamagotchi sleep rule applied to the lens, so the light is asleep under its shutter by day and tending happens only at dusk and dawn. [20] (one source)
- Extreme: a single real-time night watch per session, with the day skipped, so the whole game is one watch. [13] (one source)
- Constraint: a meter that drains but never ends the run, only dims the light, so a missed chore has a visible cost with no game over. [9] (one source)
- Constraint: a signal with a cost, so the beam can be used too much and has to rest. [11] (one source)

## Contradictions
- Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera) shares the lighthouse-as-upkeep brick. [6] (context: Mainstream helper's reading of the Steam store page, focused on the lighthouse as the home base and its repairs.) — but Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera) has no lighthouse, light or signal bricks. [7] (context: Disconfirm helper's reading of the same store page, focused on tending the light and signalling ships.)
- Keeper is praised for freedom to explore with no fail state, and for a slow pace. [2] (context: Player2 review of Keeper.) — but Keeper is 'not exactly a complex game', with 'too simple' first impressions and 'very little that's overly complex' puzzles. [3] (context: Gamingbible review of Keeper, by a reviewer who is a fan of puzzle solving; low challenge named as a weakness.)
- Static Dread 'never overstayed its welcome' despite its daily upkeep. [4] (context: Shacknews review of Static Dread.) — but Static Dread's rule tracking is 'needlessly frustrating', its job is 'lonely', and a search snippet says it settles into monotony. [5][16] (context: Sidequesting review of Static Dread; the monotony line is a search snippet (not opened).)
- Keeper is 91% of 1,088 reviews positive, with critic blurbs 'fresh and inventive'. [1] (context: Keeper's Steam store page (review ratings).) — but Keeper had 'only 140 active players' at time of writing, peak 165 at launch. [17] (context: Gamereactor article on Keeper's Steam player numbers; gives no cause.)
- Keeper's beam is aimed with the second stick. [2] (context: Player2 review, describing the aim control.) — but Keeper's light is focused with the right trigger. [3] (context: Gamingbible review, describing the light-focus control; the two reviews may describe different parts of the control.)
- Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera) has 'Very Positive' from 338 reviews, 80% positive. [7][6] (context: Steam store page snapshot.) — but Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera) shows 'Mostly Positive' from 427 reviews. [15] (context: Steambase snapshot dated 11/9/2026; counts differ by snapshot, and no review text is shown on either page.)
- A search snippet says there is 'no real incentive to interact with the lighthouse other than what you self impose'. [16] (context: Steam community review snippet for Stratera (not opened).) — but A search snippet calls it 'a pleasant little indie game'. [16] (context: Another Stratera review snippet (not opened).)
- Children felt attached to the Tamagotchi and a sense of loss when it died. [20] (context: Mental Floss account of the 1996 toy's routine.) — but Children over-invested, and the school banned the toys. [20] (context: Same Mental Floss account; the same routine produced the opposite outcome in the school setting.)
- Keeper is praised as 'fresh and inventive' and 'a psychedelic exploration of life'. [1] (context: Critic blurbs on the Keeper store page.) — but Keeper is 'lacking a little in depth'. [14] (context: TechRadar headline only; the article body was not read.)

## Assumption scoreboard
2 supported · 0 contradicted · 1 no evidence
- Supported: "It becomes a chore with nothing to look forward to." (desirable, a fear) — Chores are named as the complaint in The Lightkeeper review ('mostly mundane chores'), and a snippet calls Static Dread's upkeep repetitive (unverified). Keeper Lit is a daily checklist with no player reaction on record. Against it: Static Dread's Shacknews reviewer says it 'never overstayed its welcome', and Lighthouse Keeper (Stratera) is 80% positive despite thin duties. No source tests a no-fail daily loop, so the fear is named by sources, not measured. [12][16][8][4][7]
- Supported: "Too little to do, so the cosy feel turns into boredom." (viable, a fear) — Keeper is called 'too simple' and 'not exactly a complex game', with 'very little instruction on what your next move should be'; The Lightkeeper has a slow first half; Cagibi says the beginning can be 'easy/boring'; a TechRadar headline says 'lacking a little in depth'. Against it: the Keeper reviewer named low challenge but is a fan of puzzle solving, and the Gamereactor low player count gives no cause, so it does not show boredom. [3][2][12][11][14][17]
- No evidence: "Hard to keep the light and the sea reading clearly on a phone screen." (feasible, a fear)

## Surprises
- The real keeper's job already has a clock ritual: the weight is wound and released at the moment the lamp is lit, and each keeper stood a 4-hour night watch rotated daily. [13]
- A routine that feels good can spill into the player's real day: the Tamagotchi was banned from school, and children asked parents to care for the pets during the day. [20]

## Open questions → probes
- Does a nightly, timed lens-and-lamp routine feel like a purpose rather than a chore when there is no failure state? → playtest (timebox: half a day)
- Does a night of lamp-tending feel like a chore after 20 minutes, or like a job with a payoff? (One dusk-to-dawn loop, one chore, one ship.) → sketch (timebox: half a day)
- Does a daily upkeep loop with no fail state hold interest past the first hour, or does it turn into a checklist? (Creative plays a 20-minute slice.) → playtest (timebox: half a day)
- Can a player read a steady beam, a fog-bell pattern and a ship's position on a phone-sized screen at the same time, with the lens and ships separated? → sketch (timebox: 1 hour)
- Can the beam be aimed and held on a lens or ship on a phone without fine thumb control? → sketch (timebox: 1 hour)
- Does the lamp's fuel and wick drain at a rate that reads as a gentle task rather than a meter to watch? → proto (timebox: 1 hour)
- Does a fixed daily rhythm (watch, lamp lit at dusk, shutter by day) feel like a ritual or a chore? → sketch (timebox: 1 hour)
- Can a player tell two light rhythms apart by eye on a phone screen at night? → sketch (timebox: 1 hour)
- How many distinct light rhythms must exist before a neighbour's light is confused with yours, balanced against how many lights share a coast? → proto (timebox: 1 hour)
- How many decisions per night keep the work from feeling too thin, without a failure state? → proto (timebox: 1 hour)
- Is the idle part of the loop (waiting for dusk, a quiet morning) enough, or does the game need a visible second layer of tasks? → ask the creative (timebox: one question in the next /define)
- What do players of Keeper and Lighthouse Keeper praise and complain about in their own words? The fetched pages give only aggregates and a headline. → ask the creative (timebox: 15 minutes (creative reads two sets of Steam reviews and reports back))

## So what (draft for Define)
- The closest sourced games each share a different subset of the lighthouse bricks: The bricks are spread across several sources and no single game is a full match, so any combination would be assembled from partial precedents rather than copied from one game. [1][8][6]
- Two bricks have little or no game precedent in these sources: The clockwork and fog-bell bricks have a real-world precedent but little game precedent in these sources, so they would be new ground in play and need checking rather than copying. [13][8]
- Players praise mood, freedom from failure, and clear endings: Praise clusters on atmosphere, freedom from failure and endings, not on the chores themselves, which suggests players reward the mood and the close. [2][12][5]
- Players complain about chores with no visible purpose, thin challenge, and hard-to-read controls: The complaints fall into three kinds: tasks with no visible purpose, too little challenge or guidance, and controls or cameras that are hard to read; the first two match the creative's first two fears. [12][3][2]
- Player counts do not show that players are bored: Player counts cannot tell us whether a cosy lighthouse idea is unpopular, so the fear about boredom has to be tested by playing rather than read from sales. [17]
- Familiar anchors players already recognise: Players already know a daily checklist, a day-and-night routine and island survival, so a new lighthouse task could be placed inside one of these familiar shapes. [4][8][6]
- Hooks that players have not seen in this form yet: Each hook is a different way the lighthouse becomes more than a backdrop, and each would need its own check before it is used. [6][9][11]
- A real light's identity is its flash rhythm, drawn from a small shared set: The real precedent for a timed fog bell or flash pattern is a small shared set of rhythms, and counting that rhythm is also a readability question for fear 3. [18]
- The real keepers' jobs and tending rituals are a ready-made source of anchors: The real job already has a ritual, a rota and a record-keeping duty, and the public volunteer route offers none of these, so the historical record is the only source for them. [13][19]
- Routine toys and lighthouse-as-tool lessons show that attachment can spill over and that signals get spammed: A routine that holds attachment can also spill into the player's real day, and an unlimited signal gets spammed, so both are worth holding in mind next to the no-punishment rule. [20][11]

Draft for Define: How might we make a night at the lamp feel like a purpose rather than a chore?
Draft for Define: How might we keep the lamp and the sea readable together on a small screen?
